entries.title: Nikhilam Navatashcaramam Dashatah — overview

explanation.default: Nikhilam means working with numbers near a power-of-ten base. Instead of multiplying the large numbers directly, we multiply their gaps from the base and rebuild the product from a left part and a right part.
explanation.translation: Commonly glossed as “all from 9 and the last from 10.”
explanation.app_support: Interactive Theory/Practice for beginner/intermediate/advanced near-base ranges.

entries.title: Why Nikhilam works

explanation.default: Let B be a base such as 100. Write the factors as (B − d) and (B − e) using this app’s convention deviation = base − number. Then (B − d)(B − e) = B(B − d − e) + de. The left part is the cross-subtraction; the right part is the product of deviations, padded to the base width with carry if needed.
explanation.beginner: Near 100, the hard product becomes a small gap×gap plus a simple left number. For 98×97: gaps 2 and 3; left 95; right 06; product 9506.
explanation.intermediate: Same identity with base 1000; pad the right part to three digits.
explanation.advanced: Mixed signs (one above base, one below) still follow the identity; negative right parts need borrow/adjust.

entries.title: Nikhilam — place-value explanation

explanation.default: Think of 98 as 100 − 2. Multiplying by 97 is like taking 97 hundreds and then adjusting because of the missing 2×97. That adjustment becomes the deviation product and the cross-subtraction you see on the stage.
explanation.beginner: Start from a round hundred, then fix the leftover gaps.

entries.title: Nikhilam applicability and limits

explanation.default: Best when both factors are near the same 10^n. In this app: beginner base 100 (90–109), intermediate 1000 (990–1009), advanced 10000 (9990–10009). Outside that, prefer Urdhva.
